label: E3
title: Conservation of energy, and a system with a boundary

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Energy is a quantity that can be counted.

A system is whatever has been enclosed for the purpose of an accounting. The boundary is the closed surface that encloses it, and the surroundings are everything outside that surface. The system is chosen by the person doing the accounting.

The law of conservation of energy states that total energy is constant in any process.

Applying that law across a boundary gives the energy balance. The energy inside the boundary at the end of an interval equals the energy inside at the start, plus every quantity of energy that crossed the boundary inwards, minus every quantity that crossed it outwards.

A system’s energy changes only by energy crossing its boundary, because any other route would require the total to change. And the change in a system’s energy is fixed only once the boundary is fixed: two boundaries drawn around one situation give two different changes, both correct, because they answer two different questions.

The balance constrains the numbers and nothing else. It does not say by which route energy crossed, what caused a crossing to change, or what a quantity of energy amounts to in any unit other than a unit of energy.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Energy is never made and never destroyed. It changes form, and it moves from one place to another, and the total stays where it was.

That sounds like a rule about the world. It is. But on its own it lets you compute nothing, because it talks about the total of everything, and nobody can count everything.

So here is the move that turns it into arithmetic. Draw a line round something.

The line is closed, like a circle on paper. Whatever you have drawn round is called the system. The line itself is called the boundary. Everything outside the line is called the surroundings.

The total for inside plus outside never changes. So if the amount inside goes up, the amount outside must have gone down by the same amount. And the only way that happens is if energy crossed the line.

Step one. Split everything in two. The line is closed, so every bit of energy in the world is either inside it or outside it. Nothing is both and nothing is neither.

the total = the amount inside, plus the amount outside

Step two. Use the rule. The total does not change over the interval you are looking at. So the total at the end is the same number as the total at the start.

the amount inside at the end, plus the amount outside at the end
= the amount inside at the start, plus the amount outside at the start

Step three. Take the starting amounts off both sides. This is the move from the section on rearranging an equation, done twice. Take away “the amount inside at the start”, then take away “the amount outside at the start”. The right-hand side becomes nothing at all. The left-hand side now has four pieces in it.

You may write those four pieces in any order you like. A run of adding and taking away comes out the same whatever order you do it in. Adding 3 and then taking away 5 lands you where taking away 5 and then adding 3 lands you. So put each end value next to its own start value.

the amount inside at the end, minus the amount inside at the start,
plus the amount outside at the end, minus the amount outside at the start = 0

Now read each pair on its own. An end value minus its own start value is a change. So the first pair is the change inside, and the second pair is the change outside.

the change inside, plus the change outside = 0

The two changes add to nothing. So whatever the inside gained, the outside lost, and by exactly the same amount.

Step four. Name where it went. Energy that left the outside and arrived inside crossed the line inwards. Energy that went the other way crossed it outwards. There is no third possibility, because step one used up the whole world in two pieces.

the energy inside at the end = the energy inside at the start, plus everything that crossed in, minus everything that crossed out

Nothing was assumed there except the one rule at the top and the fact that your line is closed. It is the balance line from the section on stocks and flows, with energy as the stock.

Where you draw the line is your choice. Nothing in the situation tells you where it goes. A pan of water, a pan and its stove, a whole kitchen. Those are three different lines round one event. Each gives a different answer to “how much did the energy change?”

None of the three is the wrong answer. They are answers to three different questions, and the question is the line.

So a number for an energy change is not finished until somebody says what it was measured round. Ask “round what?” before you argue about the figure.

The warning is about what this line does not do. It tells you that the numbers have to add up. It does not tell you which way energy went. It does not tell you why a flow changed. And it does not tell you what a heap of joules is worth in kilograms of anything.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
Open OpenStax College Physics 2e, section 7.6, Conservation of Energy, at https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/7-6-conservation-of-energy. Open your browser’s find box. Type the word system and press enter.

Step 1. Determine the system of interest and identify what information is given and what quantity is to be calculated. A sketch will help.

It tells you to decide what the system is. It never tells you what a system is.

A system is not a thing in the world. It is a line somebody drew. A physics book can tell you about things in the world. It cannot tell you where you decided to draw your line.

A small gas burner heats water in a steel pan for two minutes. The gas that burns in those two minutes releases 60,000 joules of chemical energy. Of that, 42,000 joules ends up in the water and 11,000 joules ends up in the steel of the pan. The other 7,000 joules ends up in the air of the kitchen. The kitchen door and window are shut for the two minutes.

Those four figures are made up for this example.

Line one, round the water only. What crossed in: 42,000 joules, from the flame and the hot pan. What crossed out: nothing. Put that through the balance line.

The energy inside went up by 42,000 joules.

Line two, round the water and the steel pan together. Now the 11,000 joules in the steel is inside your line instead of outside it. What crossed in is the 42,000 and the 11,000 together.

The energy inside went up by 53,000 joules.

Line three, round the burner, the unburnt gas, the pan and the water. This one is different, because the chemical energy of the gas now starts inside your line. Nothing crosses in. The 7,000 joules that reached the kitchen air crossed out.

0 minus 7000 = -7000

The energy inside went down by 7,000 joules.

Check it as changes. The gas gave up 60,000 joules. The water gained 42,000 and the steel 11,000.

42000 plus 11000 minus 60000 = -7000

Line four, round the whole kitchen. The door and window are shut. Nothing crossed in, nothing crossed out.

The energy inside did not change at all. The form changed. The total did not.

Put the four side by side.

where the line is drawn change in the energy inside
the water plus 42,000 joules
the water and the pan plus 53,000 joules
the burner, the gas, the pan and the water minus 7,000 joules
the whole kitchen 0 joules

Four numbers, one event, and every one of them is right.

One joule is small. OpenStax College Physics 2e, section 7.1, puts it like this.

One joule is not a large amount of energy; it would lift a small 100-gram apple a distance of about 1 meter.

So 60,000 joules is about what you would spend lifting that apple 60,000 times. Two minutes of a small burner.

Draw the line, on paper, closed. Write on the outside of it every route by which energy can cross. The flame, the air, the light, the wire, the food, the water going down the drain. Then put a number on each route, and see whether the numbers add up to the change somebody claimed.

A balance that fails almost never fails because conservation failed. It fails because a route was left off the paper.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
No burner was measured. Only the size of the joule comes from a source, College Physics 2e section 7.1.

The shut kitchen is an idealisation and it has a time limit. Over two minutes, a closed room loses little enough through its walls that treating the crossing as zero is fair. Over an hour it is not fair, and over a day it is wrong.

So a balance that does not close has two possible causes. Either a route was left off the paper, or a figure on the paper is wrong. The balance cannot tell you which.

Conservation is exact and it is not the whole story about energy. The 7,000 joules spread through the kitchen air is every bit as real as the 42,000 in the water, and it will not cook anything. The balance counts joules. It says nothing about which joules you can still use.

The balance holds for a person exactly as it holds for a pan. What it will not do is turn joules into kilograms of a body.

points.html: An energy figure with no boundary attached is not a measurement yet. Ask “round what?” before you argue about the number.
Energy is never lost, so refuse the word when somebody uses it to close an inquiry. Energy that has left your system is in the surroundings, by some route.
A system gains or loses energy only by energy crossing its boundary. So every explanation of a change has to name a crossing.
The balance tells you the numbers must add up. It never tells you why one of them moved. So do not use conservation to explain anything.
Nothing turns joules into kilograms of a body. How much energy a kilogram of change holds depends on what the change is made of.

A person is not a closed system, so “the energy has to go somewhere” is true and names nothing. Energy crosses a person’s line inwards in food and drink. It crosses outwards as heat, as work done on things around them, and in what leaves the body unabsorbed. Two lines are both in use. One is at the mouth and skin, where unabsorbed food crosses in and back out. The other is at the gut wall, where it never crosses in. Say which one you mean.
Teach the line before the equation. A trainee who draws a closed boundary and lists the crossings can set up a problem they have never seen.
When a claim is defended on the ground that energy is conserved, say plainly what conservation does. It rules things out. On its own it establishes nothing.

blocks.prompt:
Without looking back, write down the balance line for energy across a boundary, in words.

Then say, in one sentence each, what it rules out and what it cannot tell you.
blocks.answer:
The balance line, in words. Start with the energy inside the boundary at the start. Add everything that crossed the boundary inwards. Take away everything that crossed it outwards. What you are left with is the energy inside the boundary at the end.

What it rules out: any change in the energy inside that did not happen by something crossing the line. There is no other route, so a proposed mechanism that adds no crossing cannot change the balance.

What it cannot tell you: which route energy took, or why a crossing changed size. It also cannot tell you what a quantity of energy is worth in any unit other than a unit of energy.

One thing to check in your own answer. Did you write “inside the boundary” rather than just “inside”? The line is the part people drop, and it is the part that makes the sentence mean anything.

blocks.prompt:
A note about a community kitchen contains this line.

We measured the gas going in and the heat going into the food. Only about two thirds of the energy reached the food, so a third of the energy was lost. The burners are faulty and should be replaced.

The kitchen and the figures are made up for this exercise. Say what is wrong with the reasoning, and say what you would ask for.
blocks.answer:
Two separate things are wrong, and the first one is a word.

The word “lost” is doing damage. Energy does not leave the accounts. The third of the energy that did not reach the food went somewhere. The note has not said where. So it has reported that the writer stopped counting, dressed up as a finding.

Redraw the line and the sentence changes. Put the boundary round the food, and that third crossed out of it. Put it round the whole kitchen, and the flue is a hole in your line, so somebody has to say how much went up it. That third is in the air, in the steel of the pans, in the walls, and in whatever went up the flue. Name those routes and you have an account. Do not name them and you have a gap.

The second thing wrong is the conclusion. A fraction reaching the food is not by itself evidence of a fault, because no figure has been given for what a working burner does. A number becomes a finding only when it is compared with something.

What to ask for. First, the routes: how much went up the flue, how much into the pans, how much into the room, measured or at least estimated separately. Second, the same measurement on a burner known to be in good order, so that the two thirds has something to be worse than. Third, the time over which each figure was taken. A boundary treated as sealed is only sealed for a stated stretch of time.

And one thing to say out loud. The energy in the room is real energy and it is no use for cooking. That is a fair complaint about a kitchen. It is not the same complaint as energy going missing, and only one of the two is possible.

blocks.prompt:
A journalist has three minutes and no jargon. They have read this: “the body obeys the laws of physics, so weight is just energy in minus energy out”. They want to know whether it is true.

Say what you would tell them, and give them one quotable sentence.
blocks.answer:
Three minutes, no jargon, and they need a line they can print. Say yes and no in that order, because the yes is the easy half.

The yes. Energy really is never made and never destroyed. Draw a line round a person and the energy inside that line can only change by energy crossing it. That much is arithmetic and nobody serious argues with it.

Now the no, and keep it concrete. That sentence has two words in it that are not doing what they look like they are doing.

The first is “out”. Energy leaves a person by several routes at once. It leaves as heat. It leaves as work done on things around them. And it leaves in what passes through the body without being absorbed. “Out” is a list, not a number, and the list has to be measured route by route.

The second is “weight”. Weight is measured in kilograms and energy is measured in joules, and the balance line never converts one into the other. To do that you would have to say what a kilogram of change in a body is made of. That is a question about bodies, not about physics. So the physics does not hand them the sentence they read. Something else has to, and that something else is evidence.

The quotable sentence: “Energy in minus energy out is a ledger, not an explanation. It tells you the numbers have to add up. It never tells you why one of them moved.”

What not to offer: a figure for how many kilocalories make a kilogram. You do not have one, and a number given to fill a pause is the part that gets printed.

blocks.prompt:
A system holds 1,200 at the start of an interval. Over that interval 450 crosses in and 610 crosses out.

Work out the amount inside at the end, and the net crossing.
blocks.answer:
Use the balance line. The amount inside at the end is the amount inside at the start, plus what crossed in, minus what crossed out.

1200 plus 450 = 1650
1650 minus 610 = 1040

One thousand and forty inside at the end.

The net crossing is what came in minus what went out.

450 minus 610 = -160

Minus 160 over the interval. It is negative, in the way the section on counting showed you, and the amount inside fell by exactly that much.

Check it in one line.

1200 plus 450 minus 610 = 1040

blocks.prompt:
Each row below is one boundary over one interval. Two of the four numbers in each row are given. Work out the missing one.

inside at the start crossed in crossed out inside at the end
900 300 100
900 300 1050
900 250 1100
900 0 0
blocks.answer:
The same line does all four, run forwards in the first row and backwards in the rest.

First row. Start, plus in, minus out.

900 plus 300 minus 100 = 1100

Eleven hundred inside at the end.

Second row. The end is given, so work out what must have crossed out. Start plus in comes to this.

900 plus 300 = 1200

Twelve hundred if nothing had left. It ended at 1,050, so the difference is what crossed out.

1200 minus 1050 = 150

A hundred and fifty crossed out.

Third row. Now the inflow is missing. The end plus what left is what the start plus the inflow must have been.

1100 plus 250 = 1350
1350 minus 900 = 450

Four hundred and fifty crossed in.

Fourth row. Nothing crossed either way, so nothing changed.

900 plus 0 minus 0 = 900

Nine hundred at the end. Notice what the fourth row does and does not say. The amount inside is unchanged because nothing crossed the line. That is a different situation from an amount unchanged because two large crossings matched, and the end figure alone cannot tell the two apart.

blocks.prompt:
A kerosene lamp burns in a room for an hour. The kerosene releases 900,000 joules of chemical energy in that hour. Of that, 840,000 joules ends up warming the air and the walls of the room, and the rest leaves through the window as light. The room is otherwise shut.

The lamp, the room and both figures are made up for this problem.

Work out how much energy leaves through the window. Then give the change in the energy inside each of these three boundaries, with its unit, and say for each one what crossed.

  1. Round the kerosene in the lamp.

  2. Round the lamp, the air and the walls together. Count the window as a hole in the boundary.

  3. Round the room and everything outside it that the light reaches.
blocks.answer:
First the light, which is what the hour’s energy did not leave in the room.

900000 minus 840000 = 60000

Sixty thousand joules leaves through the window as light.

Now take the three boundaries one at a time, and for each one ask what crossed it.

a) Round the kerosene. Over the hour the kerosene gives up 900,000 joules of chemical energy. All of it crosses out of that boundary, into the flame and from there into the air, the walls and the light. Nothing crosses in.

0 minus 900000 = -900000

The change is minus 900,000 joules.

b) Round the lamp, the air and the walls. The chemical energy of the kerosene starts inside this line, so it is not a crossing. Nothing crosses in. The only crossing is the light going out of the window.

0 minus 60000 = -60000

The change is minus 60,000 joules, and it is exactly the light. Check it as changes. The kerosene gave up 900,000 joules, and the air and the walls gained 840,000.

840000 minus 900000 = -60000

c) Round the room and everything the light reaches. Now the light is inside the line too, so nothing crosses it at all.

0 minus 0 = 0

The change is zero joules. Inside that line, 900,000 joules of chemical energy became 900,000 joules of warmth and light. The form changed and the total did not.

Read the three answers together. Minus 900,000, minus 60,000, and zero, for one hour of one lamp. Each is the correct answer to its own question, and the question is the line.

blocks.prompt:
A solar water heater sits on a roof. Over one day, 5,000,000 joules of sunlight crosses into the tank of water. At the end of the day the energy in the water is 4,100,000 joules higher than it was at the start.

The heater and both figures are made up for this problem.

Work out how much energy crossed out of the tank over the day, and say what fraction of the sunlight that is. Then say what your answer does not tell you.
blocks.answer:
Run the balance line backwards. The change inside is what crossed in minus what crossed out, so what crossed out is what crossed in minus the change inside.

5000000 minus 4100000 = 900000

Nine hundred thousand joules crossed out of the tank over the day.

Now the fraction, which is the crossing out divided by the crossing in.

900000 divided by 5000000 = 0.18

Nought point one eight, which as a percentage is 18 per cent.

0.18 times 100 = 18

Check it forwards before you trust it.

5000000 minus 900000 = 4100000

Four million one hundred thousand joules, which is the figure given.

What this does not tell you. It does not tell you by which route the 900,000 joules left. It could have gone through the tank’s walls into the air, or along the pipes. It could have gone back out from the hot surface, or in water drawn off and used. The balance fixes the total that crossed and says nothing about how many routes it was shared between.

It also does not tell you that 18 per cent is a lot or a little, because nothing here says what a well-made tank does. A fraction becomes a finding only when it is set against something.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

a burner releases 60,000 joules of chemical energy in two minutes
the water in the pan gains 42,000 joules in those two minutes
60,000 minus 42,000 = 18,000
so 18,000 joules was destroyed
energy cannot be destroyed, so one of the two measurements must be wrong
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the fourth. Nothing was destroyed. Eighteen thousand joules went somewhere the accounting did not look.

The trouble starts one line earlier, and it is a boundary that changed without anybody saying so. The 60,000 is counted round the burner and the gas. The 42,000 is counted round the water alone. Those are two different lines, so the difference between the two figures is not a shortfall. It is the energy that ended up between the two lines — in the steel of the pan, in the air, in the flue.

Write the third line out with its line named and the arithmetic stops looking alarming.

60000 minus 42000 = 18000

Eighteen thousand joules crossed out of the boundary that holds the burner and the water, and it is now in the surroundings. That is a finding about routes, not a violation.

What to do instead: put both numbers on the same boundary before subtracting. One way is to bring the pan and the air inside the line. Then nothing has crossed, and the two figures no longer need to match. The other way is to keep the line round the water. Then you need a figure for what crossed into the water, not a figure for what the gas released.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. The subtraction is correct arithmetic on two correct measurements, and the conclusion even appeals to a real law to check itself. Every part of it is careful except the part nobody wrote down, which is where each number’s line was.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

a room is shut for an hour and nothing goes in or out of the door
a fan inside the room runs for that hour on 300,000 joules of electricity from the mains
energy is conserved, so the total energy inside the room cannot change
300,000 minus 300,000 = 0
so the room cannot have got any warmer
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the third, and the word that broke it is “so”.

Conservation says the total energy is constant. It does not say the energy inside any line you happen to draw is constant. Those become the same statement only when nothing crosses the line, and here something does: the mains wire.

Go and look at the boundary. The door is shut and the window is shut, and a cable runs through the wall. Electricity crossing that cable is energy crossing the boundary, exactly as much as anything carried through the door would be.

So the balance line reads like this.

0 plus 300000 minus 0 = 300000

The energy inside the room went up by 300,000 joules over the hour. The balance does not say what form it ends in. It does remove the only support for “cannot have got warmer”, and the next section takes up where such energy ends up.

The fourth line is arithmetic with nothing behind it. It subtracts the 300,000 from itself because line three assumed the answer. Subtracting a number from itself always gives zero, and tells you nothing at all.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. The first two lines are correct, the law quoted is the right law, and the conclusion has the shape of a conservation argument. The check that catches it is the one this section asks for every time. Draw the line, then walk round it naming every route that crosses. A cable through a wall is easy to miss precisely because it is not a door.

blocks.prompt:
A wellness page says this.

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. So every kilojoule of energy in the food you eat has to end up somewhere in your body.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: the balance across a boundary drawn round a person, with every crossing named. The claim rests on conservation, so the way to test it is to use conservation properly.

Draw the line round the person, at the mouth and skin. Then list the routes by which energy crosses it. Inwards: food and drink. Outwards: heat leaving the body to the air and to whatever it touches. Also work done on things outside the body. Also the energy in everything that leaves the body unabsorbed.

Now put the balance line on that.

the change in the energy inside = the energy in, minus the energy out

Take a day where 9,000 kilojoules crosses in with food, 1,000 kilojoules leaves unabsorbed, and 7,600 kilojoules leaves as heat and work. All three figures are made up, to show the shape.

1000 plus 7600 = 8600
9000 minus 8600 = 400

Four hundred kilojoules stays inside. Not 9,000. The word “somewhere” in the claim was doing the work of four routes, three of which point outwards.

What this does not establish. It does not establish that the answer is 400 rather than some other figure, because the three numbers are invented and this section measures nothing. The shape is the finding. The size is not.

It does not establish anything about weight. The answer is in kilojoules. Weight is in kilograms. Nothing in the balance converts one to the other. Doing so would mean saying what a kilogram of change in a body is made of.

And it does not establish that the crossings are independent of each other. The balance holds whatever they do. Whether changing one of them leaves the others where they were is a question about bodies. The subject booklet on energy balance is where it is asked.

What to say instead of the page’s sentence. Energy in food that is not stored has left the person by a route you can name. Naming the routes is the entire content of the claim.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague says this in a meeting.

The label says this packet holds 1,200 kilojoules. So eating it puts 1,200 kilojoules into the person.

The packet and the figure are made up for this problem. The figure on the label was calculated with the Atwater general factors.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: whether the question the label’s figure answers is the same question the colleague is asking. That is the only question here, and it is answered by drawing both lines.

The label’s line. The figure was calculated with the Atwater general factors. The section before this one showed that those factors already have average losses taken out. These are what is lost in digestion, in absorption and in the urine. So 1,200 kilojoules is an estimate of what an average person gets from the packet. It is not everything the packet holds.

The colleague’s line. This one is drawn round a person, and the sentence is about this person. This person’s losses need not be the average ones. Call the gap between this person’s losses and the average D, because nobody in the room has a figure for it.

Draw the person’s line at the mouth, and the whole packet crosses in and whatever is not absorbed crosses back out. Draw it at the gut wall instead, and the unabsorbed part never crosses in. Either way the net crossing comes to the same thing.

the energy crossing into the person = 1200 minus D

Now the only honest computation available. If D is zero the colleague’s figure is right for this person, and if D is anything else it is not. Nobody in the meeting has a value for D. So the correct output of this computation is a sentence, not a number: we do not have that figure.

What this does not establish. It does not establish that 1,200 is wrong. It is very likely the right answer to the question the label was answering.

It does not establish how big D is, or even which way it points. This section gives you no way to find out. It only shows you that the two questions differ, so a figure is needed.

And it does not establish anything at all about the person’s weight. That would need a second balance, in kilograms. It would also need a claim about what any change is made of, and the ground floor does not carry that claim.

What to say in the meeting. The number is fine and the sentence is not. The label estimates what an average person gets from the packet. The claim is about what crosses into this person. Those are two different questions, and the difference between them is a quantity somebody has to measure rather than assume away.
